title: Ten years early, or three times more?
hook: Ana saves for 10 years and stops. Ben saves three times as much, later. Who wins?

knows: that compounding makes later decades grow more (compound-interest lesson)
doesNotKnow: that time to compound can be worth more than the amount contributed
how quickly a late start erodes the advantage of saving more

misconception: Whoever puts in more money ends up with more.
objective: The learner can explain that in a compounding model early deposits have the most years to grow, so a saver who starts earlier and stops can end ahead of one who starts later and puts in far more.

claims.text: Saving a fixed amount at the end of each year for n years at rate r gives deposit × ((1 + r)^n − 1) / r.
claims.source: Future value of an ordinary annuity: sum of deposit × (1 + r)^k for k = 0 … n − 1. Standard result, e.g. Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, ch. 2.

claims.text: Ana ($2,400 a year for years 1–10, then nothing) has about $252,000 after 40 years at 7%.
Ben, waiting 10 years and then saving $2,400 a year for 30 years at 7%, has about $227,000 after 40 years.
Ana puts in $24,000; Ben, waiting 10 years, puts in $72,000, three times as much.
Ben falls behind Ana once he waits 9 years (about $244,975 from $74,400 of deposits); waiting 8 years he still ends ahead (about $264,524).
At 7% a year, 30 years of growth multiplies a dollar about 7.6 times.
The lesson is a model: a fixed 7% a year, deposits at the end of each year, no fees, taxes or inflation. It is not a forecast of returns or advice.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx.

recall.question: At a steady 7%, Cat saves $1,000 a year from 25 to 35, then stops. Dev saves $1,000 a year from 35 to 65. At 65, who likely has more?
options: Dev, he saved three times as much
Cat, her money had more years to grow
recall.why: Cat's deposits compound for 30 extra years, multiplying each dollar about 7.6 times at 7%, which outweighs Dev's larger total.
